items.prose: A trading app uses a 6-digit PIN. The firm bans repeated digits, so 112233 is not allowed but 019283 is.
items.question: How many PINs are allowed?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the choices for each digit in turn, one fewer each time.

byKey.unordered: That is $\binom{10}{6}$, which ignores order. 019283 and 910283 are different PINs.
byKey.five-stages: That stops after 5 digits. A PIN has 6.

explain.text: The digits are 6 stages with 10, 9, 8, 7, 6 and 5 choices. So there are $\tfrac{10!}{4!} = 151{,}200$ PINs, about 15% of the $10^6$ codes with repeats allowed.

items.prose: A screen picks 4 of 12 stocks at random for a portfolio, every set of 4 equally likely.
items.question: What is the chance that both AZN and GSK are picked? Give a fraction.

widget.label: Chance, as a fraction
widget.accept: any form equal to $\tfrac{1}{11}$, such as $\tfrac{45}{495}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the sets with both stocks, over all sets of 4.

byKey.one: That is the chance AZN alone is picked. GSK must be picked too.
byKey.square: That is $(\tfrac{1}{3})^2$, as if the two picks were independent. Without replacement they are not.
byKey.ordered-mix: You counted all portfolios in order but the good ones without. Use one kind of count.

explain.text: Sets with both: fix AZN and GSK, then choose 2 more from the other 10: $\binom{10}{2} = 45$. All sets: $\binom{12}{4} = 495$. So the chance is $\tfrac{1}{11}$; check: $\tfrac{4}{12} \times \tfrac{3}{11} = \tfrac{1}{11}$.

items.prose: Three cards are dealt from a shuffled 52-card deck without replacement.
items.question: What is the chance all three share a suit? Give a fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The first card sets the suit; the next two must match it.

byKey.one-suit: That is the chance all three are hearts. Any of the 4 suits will do.
byKey.replaced: That is $(\tfrac{1}{4})^2$, which puts the cards back.
byKey.fixed: You kept 52 cards on every draw. The deck shrinks to 51, then 50.

explain.text: The first card can be anything. The second matches its suit with chance $\tfrac{12}{51}$, the third with $\tfrac{11}{50}$. So the chance is $\tfrac{132}{2550} = \tfrac{22}{425}$; counting gives $\tfrac{4\binom{13}{3}}{\binom{52}{3}} = \tfrac{1144}{22100}$, the same.

items.prose: Each of 4 desks must get at least one of $n$ identical orders, with $n \ge 4$. The count is $\binom{n-1}{3}$: 3 bars in the $n - 1$ gaps. Use $\binom{m}{3} = \tfrac{m(m-1)(m-2)}{3!}$, the ordered picks over $3!$, with $m = n - 1$.
items.question: Write the number of routings as a polynomial expression in $n$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $m = n - 1$ into $\tfrac{m(m-1)(m-2)}{6}$.

byKey.empty-allowed: That is $\binom{n+3}{3}$, which lets a desk get nothing.
byKey.no-divide: You kept the ordered picks of bar places. Divide by $3! = 6$.
byKey.distinct: That treats the orders as different. They are identical.

explain.text: Substituting $m = n - 1$ gives $\tfrac{(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)}{6}$. Checks: $n = 4$ gives 1, one order each; $n = 7$ gives $\binom{6}{3} = 20$. For $n = 1$, 2 or 3 it gives 0, as it should.

items.prose: Ten identical lots go to brokers A, B and C. Broker A has a minimum order of 2 lots; B and C may get none.
items.question: How many allocations are possible?

feedback.correct: Give A 2 first, then share 8 freely: $\binom{10}{2} = 45$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Hand A its 2 lots first, then share what is left with stars and bars.

byKey.ignore-min: That is $\binom{12}{2}$, which ignores A's minimum.
byKey.subtract-one: You gave A only 1 lot first. The minimum is 2.
byKey.all-min: You gave every broker 2 first. Only A has a minimum.

explain.text: Give A its 2 lots first. The other 8 lots are shared freely among 3 brokers: 8 stars and 2 bars, $\binom{10}{2} = 45$. Each allocation with A at 2 or more matches exactly one of these.

items.prose: A backtest has 20 trading days. An auditor samples 5 different days at random, every set of 5 equally likely.
items.question: What is the chance the sample contains both the best and the worst day? Give a fraction.

widget.label: Chance, as a fraction
widget.accept: any form equal to $\tfrac{1}{19}$, such as $\tfrac{816}{15504}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the samples that hold both days, then divide by all samples.

byKey.replaced: You used draws with replacement and treated the two days as independent. The sample has 5 different days.
byKey.independent: That is $\tfrac{1}{4} \times \tfrac{1}{4}$. Once the best day is in, only 4 of the other 19 days are picked.
byKey.one-day: That is the chance for one of the two days. Both must be in the sample.

explain.text: Fix both days in the sample and choose the other 3 from 18: $\binom{18}{3} = 816$. All samples: $\binom{20}{5} = 15504$. So the chance is $\tfrac{1}{19}$, which matches $\tfrac{5}{20} \times \tfrac{4}{19}$.

items.prose: Prove Pascal's rule, $\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n-1}{k-1} + \binom{n-1}{k}$, for $1 \le k \le n - 1$, by counting one set of choices in two ways.
items.question: Put the lines of the proof in order.

lines.text: Fix one of the $n$ items and call it $x$; $\binom{n}{k}$ counts all groups of $k$
Groups containing $x$ need $k - 1$ more from the other $n - 1$: $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ of them
The remaining groups avoid $x$, so all $k$ come from the other $n - 1$: $\binom{n-1}{k}$
Every group falls in exactly one of these two lists, so the lists add up to all groups

feedback.correct: Split the groups by whether they contain $x$, then add.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fix an item, count the two kinds of group, check they do not overlap, then add.

byKey.without: The groups that avoid $x$ are "the remaining" ones, so they come after the groups containing $x$.
byKey.split: The two lists must be counted before you can say they cover everything once.

explain.text: Every group of $k$ either contains $x$ or not, never both. With $x$ we choose $k - 1$ more from $n - 1$; without it, all $k$ from $n - 1$. Adding the two counts gives all groups, which is Pascal's rule: each entry is the sum of the two above.

items.title: Bootstrap or split
items.prompt: A strategy has 20 daily returns, one of them the worst day of the year. (a) A bootstrap resample draws 20 returns **with replacement**, recording the order. How many resamples are possible? (b) A random split puts 10 days in a training set and 10 in a test set. Every split is equally likely. How many splits are there? (c) Find the chance the worst day is missing from a bootstrap resample. Then find the chance it is missing from the training set of a split. (d) Explain which draws are independent, and what that means for a risk estimate.
items.model:
**(a) Bootstrap resamples.** Each of the 20 draws can be any of the 20 days, since the drawn day goes back. By the multiplication rule there are $20^{20} \approx 1.05 \times 10^{26}$ ordered resamples.

**(b) Splits.** A split is fixed by choosing which 10 days go into training; order inside a set does not matter. So there are $\binom{20}{10} = 184{,}756$ splits.

**(c) Bootstrap.** One draw misses the worst day with chance $\tfrac{19}{20}$. The bag is restored after every draw, so the 20 draws are independent and we multiply: $P(\text{missing}) = \left(\tfrac{19}{20}\right)^{20} \approx 0.358$.

**(c) Split.** Training misses the worst day exactly when it is chosen from the other 19 days: $\dfrac{\binom{19}{10}}{\binom{20}{10}} = \dfrac{92{,}378}{184{,}756} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. By symmetry the worst day is equally likely to be in either half.

**(d) Independence.** Bootstrap draws are with replacement. The bag is restored after every draw, so no draw changes the chances on any other: the draws are independent. A day can appear several times, or not at all. The split draws without replacement, so each day is used exactly once. Those draws are dependent: once the worst day is in training, no later draw can pick it.

**Consequence.** About 36% of bootstrap resamples never contain the worst day. A drawdown or VaR estimate from one such resample understates tail risk. Averaging over many resamples spreads this out. In a split, the worst day always lands in exactly one of the two halves.

rubric.text: (a) Uses the multiplication rule with replacement: $20^{20}$
(c) Split: $\binom{19}{10} / \binom{20}{10} = \tfrac{1}{2}$, with a counting or symmetry argument
(d) Says bootstrap draws are independent and split draws dependent. Links this to resamples that miss the tail days

items.prose: Each process below makes two draws.
items.question: In which are the two draws independent? Select all that apply.

options.text: Dealing two cards from one deck
options.why: The first card leaves the deck, so the second draw's chances change.

options.text: Two draws of a bootstrap resample
Picking two different analysts for a committee
options.why: The first analyst cannot be picked again, so the second pick depends on the first.

feedback.correct: For independent draws, no result changes the chances on the next draw.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the first draw changes what the second can be.

explain.text: A die and a bootstrap restore everything before each draw, so no result changes the next draw's chances. Dealing cards and picking different analysts are without replacement. Their second draw depends on the first.
